idiom_name: NULL/zero placeholder plus a hand-written do-nothing callback
implementation_notes: C has no absent value for by-value parameters and no way to invent an object, so the placeholder is chosen per slot: NULL (or a zero-initialised struct) for pointer parameters, 0 for scalars, and a hand-written function with an empty body for callback slots, declared static and file-local in the test. The friendliest shape is an API that takes a void *userdata next to its callbacks: pass NULL and never read it in the handlers the test supplies. The callee-side convention is the mirror image - (void)param; marks a parameter the implementation deliberately ignores and silences -Wunused-parameter (C23 adds [[maybe_unused]]) - but it creates no dummy and says nothing about callers. CMock and friends generate mocks for queued expectations, i.e. they serve the stub/expectation patterns, not the placeholder case.
pitfalls: NULL compiles into any pointer parameter, so a placeholder that is read later crashes inside the SUT (SIGSEGV) instead of failing an assertion at the point where the assumption broke.

(void)param; documents the callee's intent but is invisible to callers: a signature that ignores a parameter today keeps accepting the same placeholder after the implementation starts reading it, and only the dummy's own failure reveals the change.

A zero-initialised struct passed by value can violate the callee's invariants (a zero length, a NULL name) while release builds stay silent, so a placeholder struct is the least safe form of dummy in C.
